title: "Reviewing a validation package: the decision trail"

## The ticket

Six weeks after your sysadmin stood in your office asking why one server gets a three-week
paper trail for the same patch running everywhere else (`becs-in-the-pipeline`), your Quality
Analyst (QA) — the one who rejected that patch outright, an hour before CAB (change advisory
board) — routes you two documents together: the validation impact assessment she said had to
exist before this patch could ever deploy, and a short test summary behind it. Routed to
Quality for its sign-off, and to you "for approval," in the box `qa-deliverables-and-ownership`
already told you is real: system-owner co-approver, not a courtesy notification.

You open it expecting to relitigate the fight your sysadmin already lost. Instead you get a
document that reads clean on first pass — headings filled in, a test summary attached, two
signature lines waiting for dates. Twelve targeted tests, one clear conclusion, nothing that
looks obviously wrong. Which is exactly the moment `reviewing-deviations-and-capas` already
taught you to slow down, not speed up: a document that looks this finished is the one worth
reading more carefully, not less.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

You already review a version of this document every time a system goes live: a go-live
readiness pack — UAT (user acceptance testing) sign-off, test evidence, a go/no-go record —
before it reaches CAB. You know how to read one. Did testing happen against a defined scope?
Did it pass? Is there a record someone can point to later? None of that instinct is wrong here.

Four things push past what a normal go-live pack demands of you:

**Acceptance criteria have to be fixed before testing runs, not written up afterward to match
whatever happened.** Your own change process probably tolerates a test plan that firms up as
testing proceeds. This world doesn't — `quality-system-essentials` already taught you why:
criteria decided after you know the result isn't a criterion, it's a story.

**A failure gets documented and explained, not quietly re-run until it's green.** Your UAT
process probably treats "failed, re-ran, passed" as routine — flaky test, environment hiccup,
move on. Here, an unexplained pass-on-retry is a decision-trail gap on its own, whether or not
the underlying system was ever actually at risk.

**Quality's approval is a blocking sign-off, not a stakeholder review.** Your CAB approval means
the change is safe to deploy from a service-risk read. Quality's signature here means something
closer to a second required lock on the door — `becs-in-the-pipeline` already put it plainly:
both required, neither sufficient alone.

**"Validated state" is a standing obligation, not a one-time badge earned at go-live.** A system
you shipped last year and haven't touched since can still be non-compliant today, the moment a
patch to the layer underneath it changes its behavior without anyone checking. And the
obligation to check sits with **the user of the system** — Lakeshore — not with the vendor who
wrote the patch notes. That last point is where this module's sharpest teeth are.

## The rule in plain English

A validation impact assessment and its test summary have a decision trail, the same way a
deviation and CAPA packet does, and you check it with the same instrument: the **cold-read
test** — Conclusion, Evidence, Reasoning, Criteria first, Decision trail, Loose ends — sorted
with **gap triage**: must fix before I sign, fix going forward, fine as is. Neither instrument
gets re-taught here. What changes is what you're pointing them at.

Five things this document has to show, specifically:

- **Scope against BECS's four critical functions** — eligibility, release, labeling,
  disposition — and the interfaces that carry them: instrument interfaces feeding results in,
  label printers pushing output out. Not "no impact anticipated." A statement, for each one,
  that it was actually looked at.
- **Acceptance criteria set before execution.** The protocol — what counts as pass, what counts
  as fail — approved before the tests ran, not after.
- **Failures recorded honestly.** A failed step gets a discrepancy note: what failed, why,
  what changed before the re-run. Silence isn't a pass.
- **Approval before deployment, in that order.** The dates have to show assessment, then
  approval, then implementation — not a patch already live in production while an approval
  signature is still pending.
- **A vendor's word as an input, never a substitute.** A compatibility statement or release
  notes are evidence Lakeshore can weigh. They are not, on their own, Lakeshore's own
  determination.

**Here's the boundary, stated plainly, because pretending otherwise would be worse than
naming it.** Everything above is the half of this review you can actually do today. Whether
twelve targeted tests were technically the *right* twelve — whether the test design covered
the real risk, whether targeted testing was the correct call instead of a fuller revalidation —
is a different review. It rests on validation methodology (risk-based test design, what GAMP 5
[Good Automated Manufacturing Practice] and IQ/OQ/PQ actually require) this curriculum hasn't
taught you yet; that's `csv-and-becs`, still to be built. Until it exists, when that question
genuinely matters, here's a working answer, not a shrug: route it to **Quality's validation
lead** — or whoever at Lakeshore is actually qualified to judge test adequacy — and don't let
that routing be informal. Ask to see *that* review documented, the same way you'd ask to see
any other approval documented. Your job today is the decision trail: what was decided, on what
evidence, against what criteria, by whom, in what order. Whether the testing itself was enough
is someone else's call for now, and the gap here isn't in not knowing the answer — it's in not
knowing you're not supposed to know it yet.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 11.10, introductory sentence | "Eleven point ten" | Persons who *use* closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records must employ procedures and controls ensuring their authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality. | The obligation sits on Lakeshore, the system's user — not on the vendor who wrote the patch or the release notes. A vendor's compatibility statement can't discharge a duty the regulation places on you. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(a) | "...paragraph a" | Validation of systems to ensure "accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records." | Already quoted in `becs-in-the-pipeline`: BECS doesn't earn a validated state once and keep it forever. This assessment is exactly the kind of check that standing obligation requires, every time something underneath BECS changes. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(k)(2) | "...paragraph k, sub-two" | Revision and change control procedures maintaining an audit trail that documents "time-sequenced development and modification of systems documentation." | Named as a concept only, one row, no more: sequence matters in the record itself, not just in what actually happened — the same idea behind checking whether approval dates precede deployment dates. Part 11's full audit-trail framework is Track 3's (`data-integrity-and-records`, `csv-and-becs`) job, not this module's. |

## The actual text

The obligation on the user, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.10.md` — the introductory
sentence of 11.10, never quoted earlier in this curriculum:

> Persons who use closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records
> shall employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, when
> appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records, and to ensure that the signer cannot
> readily repudiate the signed record as not genuine.

Read "persons who use" as narrowly as it's written: that's Lakeshore, operating BECS, not the
company that sold Lakeshore the operating system patch. The vendor has its own obligations as a
software manufacturer, named in `becs-in-the-pipeline`. They don't transfer to Lakeshore, and
they don't run the other direction either — Lakeshore's obligation to control its own system
doesn't get satisfied by reading someone else's paperwork about their own.

The validated-state standard, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`, reused from
`becs-in-the-pipeline`:

> (a) Validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance,
> and the ability to discern invalid or altered records.

And the sequence-matters hook, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`, named once as a
concept and left there:

> (k)(2) Revision and change control procedures to maintain an audit trail that documents
> time-sequenced development and modification of systems documentation.

AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework sits on top of both, paraphrased only from
`sources/aabb/qse-framework.md`, no standard number: **Equipment** (QSE 3) covers qualification
of equipment, explicitly including IT systems — the theme behind treating a patch to BECS's
server the same way you'd treat requalifying a piece of lab equipment. **Process Control**
(QSE 5) covers validation as part of controlling a regulated process — the theme this whole
document exists to satisfy.

## The package on your desk

Here it is, exactly as routed — two signature lines, one still blank, waiting on you:

> **LAKESHORE BLOOD CENTER — VALIDATION IMPACT ASSESSMENT**
>
> **VIA ID:** VIA-0842 &nbsp;|&nbsp; **System:** BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software),
> application server &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Change:** Vendor-released OS security patch (medium-severity
> CVE, per vendor advisory); no BECS application code modified.
> **Requested by:** IT Operations &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Prepared by:** Quality Analyst &nbsp;|&nbsp;
> **Date opened:** Fri 11/06
>
> **Critical functions reviewed:** Eligibility, release, labeling, disposition. No impact
> identified.
>
> **Impact determination:** No impact to BECS's validated state. Vendor release notes state the
> patch addresses OS-level memory handling only, with no application-layer changes. Vendor's
> compatibility statement confirms support for the current BECS application version.
> **Conclusion: approved for production deployment.**
>
> **Test summary (BECS-TS-0842):** 12 targeted test cases executed, covering donor-eligibility
> lookups, quarantine/release transactions, and label-print jobs at the primary print station.
> Test scope selected in place of full revalidation, on the basis that the vendor characterizes
> this patch as OS-level only. *Scope and rationale reviewed: Quality Validation Lead, 11/06.*
>
> **Execution:** Mon 11/09 – Tue 11/10. 11 of 12 steps passed on first execution. Step 7
> (label-print job timing, primary print station) failed on first run; re-run same day, passed.
>
> **Protocol approval (acceptance criteria):** Wed 11/11.
>
> **Approvals:**
> Quality (blocking approver): Quality Analyst — **Date:** 11/12
> System owner: Director, IT Service Operations — **Date:** __________
>
> **Production deployment (per BECS change record):** Wed 11/11, 10:15 p.m.
>
> **Open items:** BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to follow.

**Before you read on: run the cold-read test yourself. Find the gaps — and separately, notice
which question in this document you genuinely can't answer yet, no matter how carefully you
read it.**

## The reveal

By the six questions, not by the document's own order.

**Conclusion.** Clean. One conclusion, stated plainly: no impact to the validated state, approved
for production. No gap here, worth saying outright — not every bucket has a hit, and pretending
otherwise trains defensive writing on the next draft.

**Evidence.** This is where the document is thinnest, in two connected ways.

First: "no impact to BECS's validated state" rests on the vendor's release notes and
compatibility statement. That's your QA's pattern again, in a new document — stopping at the
first credible-sounding source. A vendor's release notes are a real input; they're the vendor's
own characterization of its own product, not Lakeshore's independent determination. The
regulation is specific about whose obligation this is: "persons who use" the system, not the
company that patched it. Nothing here shows Lakeshore actually confirmed the vendor's claim
against BECS's own behavior — it shows Lakeshore read the claim and agreed with it.

Second: "critical functions reviewed: eligibility, release, labeling, disposition — no impact
identified" names the four functions without showing any of them were individually checked.
Compare that to the test summary right below it: eligibility lookups and release transactions
get a line each. Labeling gets one, indirectly, through the print-job test. **Nothing tests an
instrument interface at all** — the channel carrying results in, not just labels out — despite
the assessment's own header listing "critical functions reviewed" as if it had. A document can
name a scope without demonstrating it covered that scope, and this one does exactly that.

Triage: **must fix before I sign.** The conclusion may well be right. Nothing on the page proves
it yet.

**The boundary, right here — a question you can't answer from this document, and shouldn't try
to.** Twelve targeted tests, not a full revalidation. Was that enough? You don't know, and this
module hasn't equipped you to know — that's `csv-and-becs`'s job, not yours today. What you
*can* check is narrower and sits right there in the document: is the reason twelve was chosen
written down, and did someone qualified to make that call sign it? Here, yes — "scope and
rationale reviewed: Quality Validation Lead, 11/06." That's not nothing. A learner who flags
"only twelve tests" as the finding has found the wrong gap; the actual finding, if there were
one, would be an undocumented scope decision, not a small number by itself. This document
doesn't have that gap. Notice it, and move on.

**Reasoning.** Step 7's failure — the label-print job timing test — failed on first run,
re-ran the same day, passed, with no discrepancy note anywhere in the summary: no stated cause,
no explanation of what, if anything, changed before the re-run. This isn't a citation-grade
finding — Part 606's good-documentation-practice clauses are scoped to collection, processing,
testing, storage, and distribution steps on units, not to validation test scripts, and stretching
them here would be exactly the kind of overreach `reviewing-deviations-and-capas` warned against.
Treat it instead as an industry-practice and decision-trail concern, in plain terms: a test that
fails and then passes without explanation hasn't shown you it's fixed. It's shown you it's
inconsistent, and inconsistent is its own kind of risk on a label printer specifically — the
device that puts a barcode on a bag. Triage: **fix going forward.** It doesn't undo the
conclusion by itself. It's exactly the kind of gap that becomes a real problem the next time
this pattern repeats and nobody's looking as closely.

**Criteria first.** The protocol — the document defining what counts as pass or fail — was
approved Wednesday 11/11. Testing ran Monday through Tuesday, 11/09–11/10. The bar was set
*after* the results were already known. This is the exact QSE gap `capa-root-cause-to-
effectiveness` and `change-control-for-regulated-systems` already taught you to catch: a
criterion decided once you already know the outcome isn't a criterion, it's a rationalization
with a signature on it. Triage: **must fix before I sign** — this isn't a formatting slip, it
undermines the document's basic claim to have tested against a standard instead of toward a
conclusion.

**Decision trail — the one only you're positioned to catch.** The production deployment
timestamp, from BECS's own change record, is Wednesday 11/11, 10:15 p.m. Quality's approval
signature is dated Thursday 11/12. **The patch went live before Quality approved it.** A
Quality reviewer without your access to IT's own change and server logs has no reason to go
looking for this — she'd read two dates on two different documents and have no way to know they
contradict each other unless she happened to cross-check a system log she doesn't normally
touch. You do. This is the sharpest version of the Director-only IT-evidence check this course
keeps coming back to: the gap isn't hiding in the narrative, it's hiding in the gap *between*
two records that live in different systems. Triage: **must fix before I sign.** Deployed-before-
approved isn't a paperwork lag. It's the sequence this whole review exists to verify, run
backwards.

**Loose ends.** "BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to follow," on a package already
approved for production, with no owner and no date. An open item attached to a closed,
production-deployed change is exactly the kind of thing that quietly never happens once
everyone's attention has moved on. Triage: **fix going forward** — it doesn't undo this
conclusion, but it can't stay ownerless on a document that's already shipped.

**Sending it back.** Questions, not a rewrite — the same move `reviewing-deviations-and-capas`
already modeled:

- "What did Lakeshore itself check, beyond the vendor's release notes, to confirm no impact to
  each of the four critical functions — including the instrument interfaces, not just labeling
  and release?"
- "What happened on step 7's first run, and what, if anything, changed before the re-run?"
- "Why was the protocol approved after execution instead of before it — and can we re-run this
  with criteria signed first?"
- "The change record shows production deployment at 10:15 p.m. Wednesday. Quality's approval is
  dated Thursday. Walk me through that sequence."
- "Who owns the BECS-to-hospital interface regression follow-up, and by when?"

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor pulling this file asks for the same things you just went looking for, without you
in the room to prompt them. They'll ask whether the impact assessment shows Lakeshore's own
determination or just repeats the vendor's — a file that leans entirely on a vendor statement
reads as an assessment Lakeshore never actually performed. They'll pull the protocol's approval
date and the execution dates side by side, the same way you did, because a criterion set after
results is one of the fastest findings to spot once you know to look for it. They'll ask for the
discrepancy record behind any failed-then-passed step — silence there reads as a test that
wasn't actually resolved, just repeated until it stopped failing. And they'll cross-reference the
change record's deployment timestamp against the approval signatures, because "approved after
deployed" is a sequence violation regardless of whether the patch itself ever caused a problem.
A bad answer to "why did this deploy before Quality signed" sounds like "the window was already
scheduled." A good answer is a corrected change record showing approval actually came first.

## Common traps

**"The vendor said the patch was compatible with BECS, so we're covered."** This is the trap
this module was built to name directly. No. 21 CFR 11.10's introductory sentence puts the
procedures-and-controls obligation on "persons who use" the system — Lakeshore, not the vendor
who wrote the compatibility statement. A vendor's word is real evidence you can weigh. It is
never, on its own, Lakeshore's own determination, and treating it as one is exactly how a
validation impact assessment becomes a rubber stamp on someone else's paperwork.

**"It failed once, but it passed on the re-run, so it's fine now."** Passing eventually isn't
the same as understanding why it failed first. An unexplained pass-on-retry is a decision-trail
gap whether or not the system was ever actually at risk — and on a device that prints labels
onto blood bags, "we're not sure why it worked the second time" is not a sentence you want to be
saying for the first time to an inspector.

**Judging the twelve tests instead of judging what you can actually judge.** The instinct to ask
"is twelve enough?" is a good instinct pointed at the wrong target today. You're not yet equipped
to answer that question, and guessing at it is worse than naming the boundary out loud. What you
can judge — and what this document actually needs from you — is whether the decision to run
twelve instead of a full revalidation is written down and signed by someone qualified to make
that call. Ask that question. Leave the other one to `csv-and-becs`, and to Quality's validation
lead in the meantime.

## What this means for your job

- **Before you sign, ask what Lakeshore itself checked — not what the vendor said.** A
  compatibility statement is an input. Your signature means Lakeshore verified it, not that
  Lakeshore read it and agreed.
- **Check whether the four critical functions and their interfaces are each individually
  addressed, not just named in a header.** "No impact identified" next to a list of four
  functions isn't the same as evidence for each one.
- **Treat any failed-then-passed step with no discrepancy note as a real finding**, especially
  on anything touching labeling. Ask what changed before the re-run — every time, not just when
  something feels off.
- **Compare approval dates to execution dates, and approval dates to your own deployment
  records, every time.** This is the one check in the whole package that's genuinely yours —
  Quality can't run it without your access, and IT can't run it without your judgment about why
  it matters.
- **When the real question is technical sufficiency, route it — don't guess at it, and don't
  skip it.** Send it to Quality's validation lead, and confirm that review gets documented, not
  just discussed. Until `csv-and-becs` exists, that routing *is* your answer to "was this
  enough."

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: "The vendor's compatibility statement says the patch works fine with BECS, so we're covered." True or false?

False, and this one's worth being able to cite. 21 CFR 11.10's introductory sentence places the
obligation to employ procedures and controls on "persons who use" a closed system — Lakeshore,
operating BECS — not on the vendor who wrote the patch or the compatibility statement about it.
The vendor's word is a real input to Lakeshore's own assessment. It doesn't discharge Lakeshore's
obligation to make that determination itself, any more than a contractor's word that a building
is up to code would excuse the building owner from an inspection.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A different validation package leaves the "expected results" field blank on the test protocol, filled in only after the tests ran, with a note: "results matched what was observed." Gap triage: must fix before you sign, fix going forward, or fine as is?

Must fix before you sign. This is the same criteria-set-after-results pattern you just found in
VIA-0842's protocol-approval date, in a more obvious costume: if "expected" is written to match
what was "observed," no criterion existed before the test ran at all — the test can't fail by
definition, which means it never actually tested anything. `capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness`
taught you this exact test for an effectiveness check: could this have failed? A criterion
written after the fact never could.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A different BECS change used 6 targeted tests instead of 12, with no note anywhere in the file about why 6 was chosen or who approved that scope. Is "only 6 tests" the gap you'd flag?

No — and this is the distinction this module exists to teach. You still can't judge whether 6
was technically enough; that's the same out-of-scope question VIA-0842's 12 tests raised, and
the answer is still "not yet, not by you." What *is* a gap here, and a real one: unlike
VIA-0842, this file has no documented rationale for the scope decision at all, and no qualified
reviewer's signature on it. Flag that — "who decided 6 was enough, and where's that written
down" — not the number itself. The number was never yours to judge. The missing signature is.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the decision-trail half of reviewing a validation package: scope against the four
critical functions, criteria before execution, failures recorded honestly, approvals before
deployment, and a vendor's word treated as an input, not a verdict — plus a clear line for
where your judgment stops and someone else's has to start. The next module,
`reviewing-vendor-risk-assessments`, picks up the other document your QA's CAPA from
`reviewing-deviations-and-capas` promised: her reassessment of the BECS vendor itself, focused
on change notification. It's scoped the same way this one was — the decision trail you can
review today, with its own boundary named plainly where technical depth isn't yet taught.
